features.claim: Tyrannosaurus was a bipedal carnivore with a massive skull balanced by a long, heavy tail.
features.quote: Like other tyrannosaurids, Tyrannosaurus was a bipedal carnivore with a massive skull balanced by a long, heavy tail.

features.claim: Its forelimbs were short but unusually powerful for their size, and had two clawed digits.
features.quote: Relative to its large and powerful hind limbs, the forelimbs of Tyrannosaurus were short but unusually powerful for their size, and they had two clawed digits.

features.claim: The skull was extremely wide at the rear but had a narrow snout, allowing unusually good binocular vision.
features.quote: It was extremely wide at the rear but had a narrow snout, allowing unusually good binocular vision.

features.claim: The tip of the upper jaw was U-shaped.
features.quote: The tip of the upper jaw was U-shaped (most non-tyrannosauroid carnivores had V-shaped upper jaws), which increased the amount of tissue and bone a tyrannosaur could rip out with one bite, although it also increased the stresses on the front teeth.

features.claim: The teeth were robust, like lethal bananas rather than daggers, more widely spaced and also had reinforcing ridges.
features.quote: The remaining teeth were robust, like "lethal bananas" rather than daggers, more widely spaced and also had reinforcing ridges.

features.claim: The neck was exceptionally short, deep and muscular to support the massive head.
features.quote: Compared to these, it was exceptionally short, deep and muscular to support the massive head.

features.claim: The hindlimbs were among the longest in proportion to body size of any theropod.
features.quote: In contrast to the arms, the hindlimbs were among the longest in proportion to body size of any theropod.

features.claim: The tail was heavy and moderately long, in order to balance the massive head and torso.
features.quote: The tail was heavy and moderately long, in order to balance the massive head and torso and to provide space for massive locomotor muscles that attached to the thighbones.

features.claim: Preserved skin from Tyrannosaurus and its close relatives shows that these dinosaurs had scales.
features.quote: Preserved skin from Tyrannosaurus and its close relatives shows that these dinosaurs had scales.

features.claim: T. rex's height was 3.5–4.0 metres tall at the hips.
features.quote: The length of T. rex is normally estimated at closer to 12 metres long, and T. rex’s height as 3.5–4.0 metres tall at the hips.

features.claim: Tyrannosaurus had 60 saw-edged, bone-crushing, pointed teeth.

not_this.claim: The old upright, tail-dragging pose was wrong and could not have been maintained by a living animal.
not_this.quote: By 1970, scientists realized this pose was incorrect and could not have been maintained by a living animal, as it would have resulted in the dislocation or weakening of several joints, including the hips and the articulation between the head and the spinal column.

not_this.claim: The old picture of Tyrannosaurus with longer, three-fingered forelimbs like Allosaurus was wrong.
not_this.quote: For the initial mounted skeleton as seen by the public in 1915, Osborn substituted longer, three-fingered forelimbs like those of Allosaurus.

debated.claim: Whether Tyrannosaurus had feathers is debated, and there is currently no direct evidence that supports the idea of T. rex feathers.
debated.quote: However, there’s currently no direct evidence that supports the idea of T. rex feathers.

debated.claim: Whether theropods such as Tyrannosaurus had their upper teeth covered in lips is debated.
debated.quote: A conference abstract published in 2016 posited that theropods such as Tyrannosaurus had their upper teeth covered in lips, instead of bare teeth as seen in crocodilians.

debated.claim: How T. rex used its small arms is a matter of debate.
debated.quote: Compared to its overall body size, T. rex had surprisingly small arms. How it used them is a matter of debate.

second_reading.claim: The largest known Tyrannosaurus are T. rex specimens named Sue and Scotty, which jointly hold the Guinness World Record.
second_reading.quote: The largest known Tyrannosaurus are T. rex specimens named Sue and Scotty, which jointly hold the Guinness World Record.
second_reading.why: a picture could not show it

second_reading.claim: The idea that Tyrannosaurus was primarily a scavenger has been discredited.
second_reading.quote: Most paleontologists today accept that Tyrannosaurus was a predator, and the idea of Tyrannosaurus being primarily a scavenger has been discredited.
second_reading.why: a picture could not show it

second_reading.claim: The old idea that the forelimbs were useless was dismissed.
second_reading.quote: In the first detailed scientific description of Tyrannosaurus forelimbs, paleontologists Kenneth Carpenter and Matt Smith dismissed notions that the forelimbs were useless or that Tyrannosaurus was an obligate scavenger.
second_reading.why: a picture could not show it

second_reading.claim: Whether Nanotyrannus is really a separate genus of tyrannosaurids is disputed.
second_reading.quote: Scientists disagree whether Nanotyrannus is really a separate genus of tyrannosaurids.
second_reading.why: a picture could not show it
